title: ITA Section 127(10.1): CCPC Enhanced SR&ED ITC Rate
keyPhrase: ITA Section 127(10.1) CCPC enhanced SR&ED ITC rate
description: Maximize your Canadian R&D claim under ITA Section 127(10.1) legislation. Learn how CCPCs qualify for the enhanced 35% SR&ED investment tax credit rate.
summary: Subsection 127(10.1) of Canada's Income Tax Act adds a 20% investment tax credit to the 15% basic rate, giving Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs)—and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, eligible Canadian public corporations—a 35% enhanced SR&ED credit on qualified expenditures up to a $6 million annual expenditure limit, fully refundable for current expenditures.

body.text: Subsection 127(10.1) of Canada's Income Tax Act adds a 20% investment tax credit to the 15% basic rate, giving Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs)—and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, eligible Canadian public corporations—a 35% enhanced SR&ED credit on qualified expenditures up to a $6 million annual expenditure limit, fully refundable for current expenditures.
Executive Overview of the Canadian R&D Tax Architecture

Canada maintains one of the most mature and generously funded statutory research and development (R&D) tax incentive frameworks among Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) nations, anchored by the federal Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program1. Administered jointly through legislative policy formulation by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the SR&ED program disburses more than $3 billion annually in tax assistance to over 20,000 claimant enterprises, approximately 75% of which are small and medium-sized businesses4. Across the federation, over 22,000 corporations annually claim federal R&D tax incentives, with more than 4,000 of those corporate claimants concentrated in the province of Quebec alone7. Rather than operating as a discretionary grant system subject to fixed parliamentary appropriations, the federal SR&ED framework functions as an entitlement-based statutory tax mechanism embedded directly within the self-assessment corporate and personal income tax system1.

The statutory architecture of the federal SR&ED program operates through a dual-mechanism design codified in the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (ITA)1. The first mechanism, governed by subsection 37(1) of the ITA, provides an immediate 100% income deduction and an indefinite pool carryforward1. Under this provision, qualifying current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, qualifying capital expenditures—are aggregated into a dedicated pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures that may be deducted in full against current-year income from a business or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years1. The second mechanism, governed by sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA, provides for Investment Tax Credit (ITC) generation and cash refundability2. Under this second pillar, qualified SR&ED expenditures generate federal ITCs at either a basic statutory rate of 15% or an enhanced rate of 35%2. Depending on the legal status of the taxpayer, prior-year taxable capital or gross revenue metrics, and whether the expenditures fall within the statutory annual expenditure limit, earned ITCs may be refunded directly in cash, applied to offset Part I federal tax otherwise payable, carried back three taxation years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years2.

Between 2024 and 2026, the Canadian federal R&D tax regime underwent its most sweeping legislative modernization in more than a decade, driven by macroeconomic concerns over lagging Canadian business productivity, intellectual property migration, and capital intensity6. Following a two-phase national consultation initiated by the Department of Finance Canada on January 31, 2024 (which closed its first phase on April 15, 2024, and its second phase on May 27, 2024) and expanded in Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation) on April 16, 2024, the federal government committed $600 million over four years beginning in 2025—with $150 million per year on an ongoing basis— before proposing major structural enhancements in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024, and expanding them further in Budget 20256. These reforms were formally enacted into law when Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3) received Royal Assent on March 26, 202610.

The enactment of Bill C-15 fundamentally altered the financial calculus of Canadian R&D tax planning across five interconnected statutory dimensions10. First, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament doubled the baseline annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million—surpassing the interim $4.5 million proposal outlined in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement—thereby raising the maximum annual federal refundable cash credit for qualifying corporations from $1.05 million to $2.1 million7. Second, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range for the expenditure limit widened from the legacy $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million7. Third, eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was extended to eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs), whose expenditure limit is reduced by reference to average annual gross revenue rather than taxable capital, and CCPCs may elect to use the same gross revenue test2. Fourth, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, capital expenditures were restored as eligible for both the Subsection 37(1) deduction and the ITC where the property is intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more of its operating time) in SR&ED2. Fifth, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a new optional pre-claim approval process allowing claimants to obtain up-front technical eligibility determinations prior to commencing R&D or incurring costs, which was operationalized through the release of revised Form T661(26), updated Schedule T2SCH31, and updated capital and shared-use equipment policies on May 25, 20261.
Statutory and Legislative Foundations of the Federal SR&ED Program
Core Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations

The legal authority governing SR&ED deductions, tax credits, overhead calculations, and compliance obligations is distributed across specific interlocking sections of the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (ITR)2. Because the SR&ED regime separates the computation of deductible R&D expenses from the computation of investment tax credits, tax auditors must trace each expenditure simultaneously through section 37 (deductibility), section 127 (credit entitlement), section 127.1 (refundability), and section 248 (technical eligibility)2.

Governs the election between the Traditional Method and Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method; restricts proxy salary base inclusions for "specified employees" (non-arm's length employees or shareholders holding 10% or more of any class of shares) to the lesser of 75% of their salary or wages and 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), and excludes bonuses or profit-based remuneration2.

Definitions of "Investment Tax Credit" and "Qualified Expenditure"

Establishes the 15% basic ITC rate, defines "qualified expenditure", "government assistance", "non-government assistance", and "contract payment", and sets out the 20-year carryforward and 3-year carryback windows for unused ITCs2.

Provides an additional 20% ITC (bringing the total enhanced rate to 35%) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the taxpayer's annual expenditure limit for CCPCs and (post-December 15, 2024) Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)2.
Expenditure Limit and Associated Group Allocation

Defines the $6 million annual expenditure limit (for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024; previously $3 million), the taxable capital ($15M–$75M) and gross revenue phase-out formulas, and mandatory allocation across associated corporations via Schedule T2SCH492.
Netting of Assistance and Time of Acquisition

Reduces the capital cost of property for ITC purposes by government and non-government assistance (qualified SR&ED expenditures are reduced for assistance and contract payments under subsections 127(18)–(20)); specifies timing rules when depreciable property or shared-use equipment is deemed acquired (available for use) for ITC calculation purposes11.

Governs cash refundability of unused ITCs earned in the year (100% refundability on the 35% enhanced ITC within the expenditure limit; 40% refundability on the 15% basic ITC for qualifying CCPCs on current expenditures above the limit and for individuals/trusts)3.

Requires that any SR&ED ITC deducted against tax payable or refunded in cash in a taxation year be deducted from the Subsection 37(1) expenditure pool in the following taxation year (or included in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(t) if the pool turns negative)2.

Establishes the formulaic overhead substitute equal to 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (reduced from 65% after 2012), along with specific salary base caps and exclusions4.
Preparer Penalties, Gross Negligence, and Criminal Offences

Imposes a $1,000 joint and several penalty for incomplete/false preparer disclosures on Form T661 Part 9, civil gross negligence and third-party preparer penalties, and criminal prosecution for fraudulent SR&ED claims9.

body.text: Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which generally conforms to the OECD Frascati Manual while enforcing strict domestic statutory boundaries2. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls within one of four enumerated categories2. The first two categories encompass scientific research: basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a), which comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, and applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b), which comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view2. The third and largest category in commercial practice is experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c), defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto4.

The fourth category, codified in paragraph 248(1)(d), encompasses eligible support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer that is directly in support of, and commensurate with the needs of, basic research, applied research, or experimental development2. Unlike core research or experimental development, support work is restricted to an exhaustive statutory list of eight specific technical activities: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research2. Any support activity falling outside these eight specific categories—or any activity within these categories whose scope exceeds what is commensurate with and directly required to resolve the core scientific or technological uncertainty—is statutorily excluded from SR&ED2. Conversely, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activity from the definition of SR&ED regardless of their technical sophistication or commercial necessity2.

body.text: Judicial Precedents and the CRA Eligibility Framework
The Landmark Test in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen

The foundational judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act was established by Justice Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 252033. In Northwest Hydraulic, the Tax Court synthesized five cumulative questions that Canadian courts and the CRA apply to determine whether a claimed activity constitutes eligible SR&ED29. Because all five questions must be answered in the affirmative for a project to qualify, failure on any single criterion is fatal to the entire project claim29.

The first question asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures3. Justice Bowman emphasized that the phrase "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field8. If the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using established methodologies or publicly available knowledge, no technological uncertainty exists, even if the engineering effort is complex, time-consuming, or commercially risky31. Furthermore, technological uncertainty must be rigorously distinguished from business or market uncertainty: not knowing whether customers will adopt a software platform is a market question, whereas not knowing whether a novel algorithm can process 10 million events per second with sub-100-millisecond latency on commodity hardware is a genuine technological uncertainty31.

The second and third questions examine the methodology of the investigation, asking whether the claimant formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, and whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses4. Satisfying these criteria requires a structured, multi-stage intellectual process: characterizing the system's underlying technical constraints, articulating a testable hypothesis explaining why the limitation occurs or how a proposed mechanism will overcome it, and executing a methodical plan of experimentation or analysis4. Ad hoc troubleshooting, undocumented trial-and-error, or intuitive debugging where developers simply try different configurations until one works fails to meet the discipline of the scientific method31.

The fourth and fifth questions evaluate the outcome and evidentiary trail of the investigation, asking whether the process resulted in a technological advancement and whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results, was kept as the work progressed3. A technological advancement represents an increase in the stock of technological knowledge or capability—including a systematic, documented understanding of why a hypothesized technological approach fails under specific boundary conditions31. Consequently, a project need not succeed commercially or even achieve its targeted performance metrics to qualify for SR&ED, provided the investigation was designed to push the boundary of what is currently known or achievable beyond standard practice31. While the Income Tax Act does not make contemporaneous documentation an independent statutory element of the definition of SR&ED, Justice Bowman underscored that detailed contemporaneous records are a natural by-product of the scientific method and are practically indispensable to discharge the taxpayer's evidentiary burden during a CRA review or Tax Court appeal3.

body.text: Evolution from the "Five Questions" to the CRA "Two Requirements" Framework and Subsequent Jurisprudence

On August 13, 2021, the CRA archived its longstanding Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy—which had explicitly structured technical reviews around the five questions from Northwest Hydraulic—and replaced it with the Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives10. The 2021 Guidelines consolidated the administrative analysis into Two Requirements, designated by the CRA as the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement33. The "Why" Requirement mandates that the work be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement by attempting to overcome a scientific or technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved through standard practice8. The "How" Requirement mandates that the work be a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, progressing methodically from identifying the obstacle and formulating clear objectives and hypotheses to executing experiments and drawing conclusions4.

Following the 2021 administrative transition, tax practitioners and litigants questioned whether the CRA's Two Requirements subtly raised or altered the substantive legal threshold established by the judiciary30. The answer lies in the jurisprudence of the Federal Court of Appeal: in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the Northwest Hydraulic test30. Because administrative guidelines issued by the CRA cannot modify the statutory meaning of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, the CRA's Two Requirements do not displace that jurisprudence, which confirms that the five-question test articulated by Chief Justice Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic remains the binding legal standard in Canada30. Consequently, the CRA updated its historical guidance note (most recently on August 27, 2025) to explicitly confirm that both the Two Requirements and the Five Questions are derived directly from the unchanged text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and provide a common language for claimants and CRA officials to evaluate SR&ED eligibility33.

Subsequent Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence further illustrates the strict interdependence of the "Why" and "How" requirements3. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, Justice D'Arcy of the Tax Court of Canada examined a claimant that had maintained thorough, well-organized contemporaneous records and demonstrated that its personnel had undertaken a structured, systematic investigation3. Despite finding that Jentel had satisfied the methodological and documentary criteria of a systematic investigation, Justice D'Arcy dismissed the appeal and denied all claimed SR&ED credits because none of Jentel's activities addressed a technological uncertainty that could not be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures3. Conversely, in cases involving multi-stage software development (such as LawBot, Inc. case analyses), courts and the CRA distinguish sharply between experimental algorithm development during the trialing phase—which satisfies the Five Question Test where new technological knowledge is generated—and subsequent commercial production or market deployment, which is statutorily ineligible3. Thus, rigorous documentation and systematic project management ("How") can never substitute for the absence of an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty ("Why")3.
Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Budget 2025 / Bill C-15 Reforms
Comparison of Pre-Reform vs. Post-Bill C-15 Federal SR&ED Parameters

The passage of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, enacted the Budget 2025 SR&ED reforms into law with retroactive effect for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, and for capital expenditures incurred after December 15, 202410. Because corporations with fiscal years that began on or before December 15, 2024, remain governed by the legacy rules for that straddling taxation year (meaning the first full wave of calendar-year corporations to benefit from the new rate and limit thresholds are those with taxation years ending in December 2025 and filing in 2026), tax auditors and corporate filers must rigorously distinguish between the legacy statutory parameters and the post-Bill C-15 regime7.

body.text: Mathematical Mechanics of the Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas

Under subsection 127(10.2) of the Income Tax Act, as amended by Bill C-15, the baseline annual expenditure limit for a CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs allocating the limit via Schedule T2SCH49) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, is $6,000,00010. Where the corporation, together with all associated corporations, has prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced linearly according to the following statutory formula2:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000.

Under this linear phase-out, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1, reaching zero when prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,0007. By contrast, under the legacy regime applicable to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada7:
Expenditure limit = $3,000,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000, where A is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $10,000,000.

Beyond widening the taxable capital thresholds, Bill C-15 introduced a major structural reform to prevent the premature clawback of enhanced SR&ED credits for capital-intensive scale-up companies—such as clean-technology, semiconductor, bio-manufacturing, and deep-tech hardware enterprises—whose balance sheets carry substantial debt or equity capital (and therefore high taxable capital employed in Canada) prior to generating significant commercial revenues2. Specifically, subsection 127(10.2) now permits a CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs) to formally elect out of the taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out structure and instead determine its expenditure limit reduction using a gross revenue-based phase-out formula2. Conversely, for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), the expenditure limit reduction is determined exclusively using the gross revenue test rather than taxable capital2. These dual phase-out tracks ensure that high-growth domestic innovators are no longer penalized merely for raising balance-sheet capital or listing on a Canadian public stock exchange13.
Comprehensive Refundability Matrix by Taxpayer Type

The cash flow impact of the SR&ED program depends critically on the interaction between the statutory ITC rate (35% enhanced vs. 15% basic), the nature of the expenditure (current vs. restored capital), and the refundability percentage governed by section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act4. Furthermore, under paragraph 12(1)(t) and paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA, any SR&ED ITC that is either refunded in cash or applied to reduce Part I tax payable in a given taxation year reduces the taxpayer's Subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the immediately following taxation year—or, if the deduction reduces the pool below zero, is included directly in the taxpayer's taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(t) in that following year2. Where a taxpayer has insufficient Part I tax liability to absorb non-refundable ITCs, subsection 127(9) permits unused ITCs to be carried back up to three taxation years (subject to annual credit application limits) or carried forward for up to 20 taxation years2.

To illustrate the divergent cash refund mechanics across corporate structures under the post-Bill C-15 rules, consider a qualifying CCPC in a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, that incurs $8,000,000 in qualified current SR&ED expenditures and retains its full $6,000,000 expenditure limit13. On the first $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures, the CCPC earns the enhanced 35% ITC, which is 100% refundable, generating $2,100,000 in immediate cash refunds13. On the remaining $2,000,000 of qualified current expenditures exceeding the $6,000,000 limit, the CCPC earns the basic 15% ITC ($300,000), of which 40% is refundable in cash ($120,000, representing an effective 6.0% cash refund rate) and 60% ($180,000, representing an effective 9.0% rate) is non-refundable, yielding a total current-year cash refund of $2,220,000 alongside $180,000 in non-refundable ITCs4. If an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) incurs the exact same $8,000,000 in qualified expenditures with a full $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the ECPC likewise receives $2,100,000 in refundable cash credits on the first $6,000,000 (at 35%), but the $300,000 basic 15% ITC earned on the $2,000,000 excess is entirely non-refundable (0% cash refundability)13. For partnerships, because a partnership is not a separate taxable entity under the ITA, SR&ED ITCs cannot be refunded to or carried forward by the partnership itself; instead, qualified expenditures and ITCs are calculated and allocated directly to eligible partners at the end of the fiscal period2.

body.text: Salaries and Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are "directly engaged" in performing SR&ED in Canada are 100% eligible for the Subsection 37(1) deduction and enter the qualified expenditure base at 100%2. In evaluating direct labour, the CRA assesses eligibility strictly based on the hands-on technical tasks performed by the individual rather than job title or corporate rank2. First-line technical supervisors who direct the technical execution of experiments qualify to the extent of their hands-on technical direction, whereas general executives, administrative personnel, human resources staff, and accounting personnel are excluded from direct SR&ED labour2. Where Canadian residents perform SR&ED work outside Canada that is directly in support of a core Canadian SR&ED project, those foreign salaries are eligible up to a maximum cap of 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages paid to employees performing SR&ED within Canada2.

Stringent anti-avoidance limitations apply under subsections 37(8), 37(9), and 37(9.1) of the ITA and Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(9) of the ITR to any "specified employee"—defined as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time during the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer corporation or any related corporation27. For specified employees, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are statutorily excluded from eligible SR&ED salaries, and total direct SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE), prorated by the number of days in the year on which the individual is a specified employee27. Furthermore, when computing the salary base for the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(7), the includable proxy salary base for each specified employee is restricted to the lesser of 75% of that employee's total eligible salary and wages and 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual is employed by the taxpayer27:

Includable proxy salary base = the lesser of (75% × eligible salary and wages) and (2.5 × YMPE × B ÷ 365), where B is the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is employed by the taxpayer.
Materials Consumed or Transformed, Subcontractors, and Third-Party Payments

Expenditures for materials qualify at 100% only if the materials are either consumed (rendered virtually value-less or destroyed during experimentation, prototyping, or testing) or transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant in a manner that alters their physical or chemical utility) during the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada2. Raw materials incorporated into commercial products intended for sale do not qualify, and if an experimental prototype or transformed material is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial production use, the SR&ED recapture provisions claw back the ITC previously earned3.

Payments for outsourced R&D are governed by the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy and Third-Party Payments Policy, both updated on October 29, 202510. Under these policies, an arm's-length SR&ED contract is a contract for the performance of basic research, applied research, experimental development, or eligible support work done in Canada on behalf of a claimant2. While 100% of an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor payment is deductible in the Subsection 37(1) pool, only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in qualified expenditures for Section 127 ITC purposes—a statutory 20% reduction designed to exclude the contractor's profit markup and prevent cascading credits2. If the subcontractor does not deal at arm's length with the claimant, the payment does not directly generate ITCs for the payer unless the parties execute a joint election to transfer the qualified expenditures using Form T1146 (updated May 25, 2026)10. Similarly, third-party payments made under paragraph 37(1)(a) to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or other organizations to carry on SR&ED in Canada related to the claimant's business (where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results) are included in qualified expenditures at 80% for ITC purposes and reported where applicable on Form T1263, provided the payment is not made to enable the recipient organization to acquire a building or a leasehold interest in a building under subparagraph 37(8)(e)(iv)2.
Restored Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Acquired After December 15, 2024)

Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, and the CRA's May 25, 2026 publication of Form T661(26), the SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, and the SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, capital property acquired after December 15, 2024, is once again eligible for SR&ED incentives under the general framework that existed prior to 20142. Under the primary capital expenditure track, an expenditure made to acquire new or used depreciable property (excluding land, which is non-depreciable, and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings, which are generally excluded) that becomes available for use after December 15, 2024, qualifies at 100% of its full capital cost—including purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other acquisition costs—if the claimant intends either to use the property all or substantially all (ASA, defined strictly as 90% or more) of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada11. Claimants must list the names and costs of the 10 most expensive SR&ED properties acquired after December 15, 2024, on Form T661 Lines 262 and 263, claim the capital expenditure on Line 390 (and Line 535 for ITC purposes), and include it in Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures on Line 40011. Because capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 enter the Subsection 37(1) pool for immediate 100% deduction, they must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 for regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA)11.

Where new (not used) depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, does not meet the 90% ASA threshold but is used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies under the restored Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) rules10. The SR&ED ITC calculation for SUE is identical under both the Traditional Method and the Proxy Method11. Unlike ASA capital property, the capital cost of SUE is not included in the Subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and must instead be depreciated under regular CCA rates and rules on Schedule T2SCH811. For Section 127 ITC purposes, if the equipment satisfies the primary-use operating requirements of first-term SUE and second-term SUE, the claimant claims 25% of the capital cost of the equipment on Form T661 Line 504 (Box 792) in the first period (first-term SUE) and another 25% of the capital cost in the second period (second-term SUE), yielding a cumulative 50% qualified expenditure inclusion11. Furthermore, for equipment leasing after December 15, 2024, lease costs for equipment used all or substantially all (90% or more) of the time in SR&ED qualify as capital lease expenditures, while under the Traditional Method, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED less than 90% of the time may be claimed on Form T661 Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures11. Note also that under subsection 127(11.2) of the ITA as amended by Bill C-15, specific time-of-acquisition rules govern when capital property is deemed acquired for ITC purposes11.
Traditional Method vs. Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method for Overhead

Claimants must elect annually on Form T661 whether to calculate SR&ED overhead expenditures using the Traditional Method or the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method, updated in the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy on October 29, 20254. Under the Traditional Method, the claimant identifies, tracks, and itemizes all overhead and other expenditures directly attributable and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada on Line 3604. By contrast, the Prescribed Proxy Amount method simplifies compliance by using a statutory formula under Regulation 2900(4) to calculate a notional substitute amount for overhead equal to 55% of the eligible proxy salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (reduced from 65%, which has not been the statutory rate since 2012)4. Because the 55% PPA is a notional inclusion solely for Section 127 ITC purposes, it does not enter the Subsection 37(1) deduction pool; instead, the claimant deducts its actual overhead expenses under ordinary business deduction rules in section 9 of the ITA4.

body.text: Treatment of Cloud Computing, SaaS, and AI Infrastructure Costs

In contemporary software-as-a-service (SaaS), data analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI) R&D, cloud computing infrastructure (such as Amazon Web Services [AWS], Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform [GCP]), third-party APIs, and GPU compute clusters represent major expenditures37. Under CRA audit guidelines and Canadian Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE), claimants must maintain strict chart-of-accounts segregation between production infrastructure and R&D infrastructure37. Cloud hosting costs and third-party API fees incurred to deliver a live commercial software product to paying customers constitute Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) / Cost of Revenue and are categorically ineligible for SR&ED3. Only cloud infrastructure, staging environments, and compute clusters dedicated to experimental development—and tracked contemporaneously via distinct AWS/GCP/Azure environment resource tags and SR&ED project codes—may be evaluated for SR&ED eligibility37.

Furthermore, claimants must distinguish between operating cloud subscriptions and capital AI hardware37. Cloud-hosted AI tools and SaaS subscriptions are operating expenses (fully deductible in the year incurred) rather than capital property37. Under the Traditional Method, directly attributable R&D cloud compute costs can be claimed as directly attributable overhead, whereas under historic CRA interpretations of the Proxy Method, general hosting utilities were subsumed into the 55% PPA—though Bill C-15 (2026) introduced modernizations expanding cloud-computing eligibility4. Conversely, when a business purchases physical AI hardware or server infrastructure (ordinarily classified under CCA Class 50 at a 55% declining-balance rate, or CCA Class 12 at 100% for purchased application software or perpetual licences) after December 15, 2024, and uses that hardware all or substantially all (90% or more) for internal AI model training or experimental development in Canada, the hardware now qualifies directly as a restored SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661(26), or as Shared-Use Equipment on Line 504 if used primarily (more than 50%) but less than 90% for SR&ED11.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island, which administers direct innovation rebates rather than a corporate income tax credit) and the Yukon Territory provides a statutory R&D tax credit or grant that stacks atop the federal SR&ED program43. Most provincial regimes are administered directly by the CRA via T2 corporate tax return schedules (providing a unified single-window audit alongside Form T661), whereas Quebec and Alberta administer their R&D incentives independently through Revenu Québec and Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, respectively43.

body.text: Mathematical Mechanics of Federal-Provincial Stacking and Government Assistance

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9) and 127(11.1) of the Income Tax Act, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (including the Ontario OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC, the B.C. SR&ED tax credit, the Quebec R&D credits, the Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, and Yukon R&D tax credits, and the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant)—as well as direct government grants and emergency wage subsidies—are statutorily classified as "government assistance"5. Any government assistance or non-government assistance that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year reduces both the Subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the Section 127 qualified expenditure base (reported on Form T661 Line 514 for provincial/territorial government assistance and Line 516 for other government assistance) prior to computing the federal ITC11. However, as clarified in the CRA's May 25, 2026 instructions for Form T661(26), claimants must exclude from Line 514 any provincial or territorial government assistance attributable to a capital expenditure incurred for depreciable property acquired and available for use before December 16, 2024, because pre-December 16, 2024 capital expenditures were ineligible federally11.

To demonstrate the precise mathematical interaction between provincial and federal credits, consider a qualifying CCPC incurring $1,000,000 in eligible current SR&ED expenditures (inclusive of the 55% proxy overhead) in a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, across two representative provinces: British Columbia and Ontario13. In British Columbia—which enacted Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) to harmonize its provincial SR&ED tax credit with federal Bill C-15 by raising the B.C. expenditure limit to $6,000,000, extending the 10% refundable credit to ECPCs, raising the taxable capital phase-out to $15M–$75M, restoring capital expenditures, and removing the provincial sunset date—the corporation first earns a 10% refundable B.C. SR&ED credit of $100,000 on Schedule 42513. That $100,000 provincial credit is deducted on Form T661 Line 514, reducing net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures to $900,000, upon which the 35% federal ITC yields $315,000, resulting in a combined refundable cash recovery of $415,000 (41.50% of the expenditure base)11.

In Ontario, a qualifying CCPC claiming both the 8% refundable OITC (Schedule 566) and the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule 508) undergoes a two-step reduction16. First, the 8% OITC yields $80,000 in refundable provincial credits16. Second, under Ontario's statutory ordering rules, the eligible expenditure base for the 3.5% ORDTC is reduced by any OITC and OBRITC claimed, leaving $920,000 ($1,000,000 minus $80,000) to earn a 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC of $32,20016. Third, both the $80,000 OITC and the $32,200 ORDTC reduce the federal qualified expenditure base on Form T661 Line 514 to $887,800, which generates a 35% refundable federal ITC of $310,730, yielding a combined federal-provincial benefit of $422,930 (42.293%)13. Notably, if an Ontario CCPC is in a non-taxable loss position and cannot immediately utilize the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC, it may file a written waiver of the ORDTC within six months of its tax year-end (or on an amended return for that year) so that the ORDTC does not reduce its 35% cash-refundable federal SR&ED ITC; waiving the $32,200 non-refundable ORDTC increases the refundable federal ITC by $11,270 ($32,200 × 35%) to $322,000, yielding $402,000 (40.20%) in pure cash refunds16.

body.text: In Quebec, provincial stacking underwent a major modernization for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, when the Quebec government abolished the legacy Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages – R&D (Form RD-1029.7) and consolidated its R&D tax incentives into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)54. Under both the legacy RD-1029.7 regime and the new CRIC regime administered by Revenu Québec, eligible R&D expenditures carried out in Quebec must first exceed an asset-based exclusion threshold that starts at a base floor of $50,000 and increases linearly up to $225,000 depending on prior-year total assets47. Above the exclusion threshold, the CRIC provides an enhanced 30% refundable tax credit rate on the first $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures and a 20% refundable rate on excess expenditures, which in turn reduces the federal qualified expenditure base on Form T661 Line 51411. Notably, despite provincial fiscal consolidation targets in Quebec seeking $2.9 billion in broader expenditure savings over five years, the Quebec government preserved the core generosity of its R&D tax credit envelope7.
Administrative Procedures, Form T661(26) Architecture, and the CRA Audit Process
Statutory Filing Deadlines and Mandatory Prescribed Forms

Unlike standard corporate tax deductions that can be adjusted through post-assessment amendment requests within the normal reassessment period, SR&ED claims are governed by a strict, non-discretionary statutory deadline under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the Income Tax Act4. A corporate claimant must file its prescribed SR&ED forms—specifically Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations, or Form T2038(IND) for unincorporated individuals), along with Schedule T2SCH49 where associated CCPCs allocate the expenditure limit—no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred4. The CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated November 26, 2020) strictly enforces this 18-month reporting deadline: if a claimant fails to submit the prescribed forms identifying the projects and expenditures within 18 months of its fiscal year-end, the claim is statutorily barred and cannot be accepted4. While corporations legally have up to 18 months after fiscal year-end to submit their claim (and B.C. Schedule 425 shares this 18-month window, whereas the Alberta IEG AT1 Schedule 14 must be filed within 15 months after the corporation's filing due date), filing the SR&ED claim simultaneously with the original T2 corporate income tax return within six months of fiscal year-end cuts CRA processing times by approximately 50%, typically delivering refunds within 60 to 90 days for claims accepted as filed5.
Detailed Structure of Form T661(26) (May 25, 2026 Revision)

On May 25, 2026, the CRA released an updated version of Form T661(26) (alongside updated Guide T4088, Schedule T2SCH31, Form T1145, and Form T1146) to operationalize the Bill C-15 legislative enhancements and the new pre-claim approval process10. Part 2 of Form T661(26) remains the technical cornerstone of the claim, requiring claimants to submit a separate Part 2 for each claimed SR&ED project25. Within Part 2 Section B, claimants must adhere strictly to the statutory word limits on the three technical narrative boxes—Line 242 (maximum 350 words on scientific or technological uncertainties), Line 244 (maximum 700 words on the systematic work, hypotheses, experiments, and analysis performed in the tax year), and Line 246 (maximum 350 words on the scientific or technological advancements achieved)—using concise, factual technical language prepared by or with the personnel who performed the work25.

body.text: The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Effective April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its new Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, fulfilling a key administrative modernization commitment from the 2024–2025 consultations1. Before commencing SR&ED work or incurring R&D costs, an eligible business may submit its proposed R&D project plan to the CRA to have the proposed work evaluated up front for technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) of the ITA1. If approved, the CRA issues a formal pre-claim approval case number that is entered on Form T661(26) when the tax return is subsequently filed10. While pre-claim approval provides early certainty regarding whether a project's technological uncertainties and proposed methodology qualify as SR&ED, participation is optional, and approved claimants must still submit a full Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 with their income tax return after year-end to substantiate the actual work performed and expenditures incurred1.
CRA Audit, Review, and Dispute Resolution Architecture

On October 29, 2025, the CRA published an updated administrative manual titled The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, formally replacing its earlier 2011 publication (The SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants)8. When an SR&ED claim is filed with a T2 or T1 return, it is initially assessed at a CRA Tax Centre8. Claims that pass automated risk screening may be accepted as filed, whereas claims selected for desk review or detailed technical and financial review are routed to a regional Coordinating Tax Services Office (CTSO)8. At the CTSO, the Control Centre assigns the file to two distinct specialists: a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), who is a domain scientist or engineer responsible for reviewing past and current technical filings, requesting supporting documentation, conducting on-site or virtual technical interviews, and determining whether the claimed projects satisfy subsection 248(1); and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who audits the general ledger, payroll records, specified employee calculations, contractor agreements, capital/SUE acquisition dates, and government assistance reductions5.

When a site visit is conducted, the RTA sends an advance agenda of activities and contemporaneous documents to be examined, interviews the lead technical personnel who performed the work, and provides a preliminary verbal indication of eligibility findings or outstanding concerns at the conclusion of the visit so the claimant has a fair opportunity to submit supplemental representations8. The RTA then formalizes the technical findings in a written SR&ED Review Report, and the FR and RTA jointly issue a CRA Proposal Letter detailing any proposed adjustments8.

If the claimant disagrees with the RTA or FR's findings during the review process, the CRA and the Income Tax Act provide a structured four-stage escalation and appeal pathway8. First, the claimant is encouraged to resolve factual or technical misunderstandings directly with the RTA and FR in response to the SR&ED Review Report and Proposal Letter8. Second, if direct discussions fail to resolve the impasse, the claimant may escalate the dispute to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or Financial Review Manager (FRM) who supervises the reviewers8. Third, if managerial review remains unsatisfactory, the claimant may request an Administrative Second Review conducted by the Assistant Director, SR&ED at the CTSO to verify procedural fairness and adherence to policy8. Fourth, once a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, the claimant has 90 days under subsection 165(1) of the Income Tax Act to serve a formal Notice of Objection on the CRA Appeals Branch, and if the Appeals Branch confirms the assessment or does not vacate it, the claimant may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada under subsection 169(1) of the ITA8.
Statutory Penalties, Preparer Compliance, and Audit Risk Mitigation
Civil and Criminal Penalty Framework under the Income Tax Act

Because the SR&ED program disburses substantial refundable cash credits, the Income Tax Act enforces a comprehensive civil and criminal penalty architecture targeting both claimants and third-party SR&ED consultants or claim preparers9. Specifically, subsections 162(5.1), 162(5.2), and 162(5.3) of the ITA enforce strict transparency regarding third-party claim preparers and contingency-fee billing arrangements in Part 9 of Form T6619. Where a false statement or omission is made in the required claim preparer information on Form T661 (such as omitting a preparer's identity or inaccurately reporting fee structures), a $1,000 penalty applies for each affected SR&ED claim, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable, subject to a due-diligence defence for the preparer under subsection 162(5.2)9. Beyond administrative preparer disclosure penalties, grossly negligent or fraudulent claims trigger severe civil penalties under subsections 163(2) and 163.2(4) as well as criminal prosecution under subsections 239(1.1) and 239(2) of the ITA9.

body.text: Contemporaneous Documentation Standards and Audit Defence Best Practices

Empirical CRA audit data and Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence consistently demonstrate that the primary reason SR&ED claims are reduced or denied during review is not the substantive ineligibility of the underlying R&D, but rather insufficient or inappropriate contemporaneous evidence3. To construct an audit-ready claim under the updated October 29, 2025 SR&ED Review Process guide and Form T661(26), claimants must embed documentation capture directly into their real-time engineering and financial workflows rather than reconstructing narratives retrospectively3.

First, technical narratives on Form T661 Part 2 must be anchored strictly in technological uncertainty rather than commercial or functional product goals25. On Line 242, authors must articulate the exact technical threshold, system limitation, or architectural conflict that could not be resolved using publicly available knowledge or standard engineering procedures, linking that uncertainty directly to the hypotheses and experimental iterations on Line 244 and the resulting knowledge gain on Line 24625. Second, claimants should capture real-time experimental evidence directly from native engineering repositories—such as GitHub or GitLab commit histories, pull requests documenting failed iterations, Jira tickets tagged with SR&ED project codes, dated benchmark logs, prototype test data, and engineering Slack channels—to prove that a systematic, hypothesis-driven investigation occurred contemporaneously5. Third, because direct labour eligibility requires hands-on engagement in SR&ED, businesses must maintain monthly or bi-weekly developer and engineer timesheets coded by specific SR&ED project to substantiate the exact split between qualifying experimental development, eligible support work, and routine commercial coding or bug fixing2. Fourth, for claimants utilizing the newly restored capital expenditure rules (Line 390) or Shared-Use Equipment rules (Line 504) for depreciable assets acquired after December 15, 2024, accounting teams must maintain dated acquisition invoices, commissioning logs proving when the equipment became available for use in Canada, and machine-hour logs demonstrating 90% or more ASA usage (or more than 50% SUE usage) in SR&ED while verifying that Line 390 assets are excluded from Schedule T2SCH8 CCA schedules11.
Complementary Federal Innovation Incentives and Ecosystem Integration

While the SR&ED Tax Incentive Program forms the statutory bedrock of Canadian R&D support, corporate tax planning between 2024 and 2026 increasingly requires coordinating SR&ED claims with direct federal grants, accelerated capital cost allowance incentives, and Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits17. In the direct funding sphere, the National Research Council of Canada's Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP) provides non-repayable contributions covering a portion of internal R&D salaries and contractor fees for innovative SMEs, complemented by Budget 2024's $2.4 billion AI package—which includes $2 billion for the AI Compute Access Fund and Canadian AI Sovereign Compute Strategy, $200 million for sectoral AI adoption, and $100 million for the NRC AI Assist Program—alongside $2 billion for the Global Innovation Clusters and $14.5 million over two years for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada's (ISED) Innovation Asset Collective18. Claimants can strategically stack NRC-IRAP grants and SR&ED tax credits on the same project: while the IRAP grant constitutes government assistance that reduces the qualified expenditure base on Form T661 Line 516, the claimant remains entitled to claim SR&ED tax credits on the unfunded portion of project expenditures (and calculates the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount on the unreduced eligible salary base before deducting the assistance)5.

For capital investments in innovation and sustainable industrial scale-up, Parliament has enacted two additional sets of tax incentives that interact with SR&ED17. First, Budget 2024 enacted an immediate 100% capital cost allowance write-off for capital investments in patents, data network infrastructure equipment, computers, and other data processing equipment acquired on or after April 16, 2024, and available for use before January 1, 2027, while Budget 2025 introduced temporary immediate expensing for qualifying manufacturing and processing buildings (which remain excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures as Class 1 buildings)11. Second, the federal government established five major refundable Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits: the Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) ITC, the Clean Technology ITC (up to 30% refundable), the Clean Hydrogen ITC, the Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC (a 30% refundable credit covering eligible property used all or substantially all in clean technology manufacturing or qualifying critical mineral extraction and processing activities producing copper, nickel, cobalt, lithium, graphite, and rare earth elements), and the Clean Electricity ITC17. While provincial clean-tech and R&D credits can stack with federal programs after netting out direct rebates, a taxpayer cannot claim both a federal SR&ED ITC and a federal Clean Economy ITC on the same capital asset cost, requiring capital-intensive enterprises to model whether claiming the asset under the restored SR&ED capital regime (35% refundable for CCPCs/ECPCs within the $6 million limit, or 15% basic rate) or under the 30% refundable Clean Technology / Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC yields the superior after-tax return11.
